brief.head: Second systems sink
brief.text: A first sys­tem is built by frail, ter­ri­fied mav­er­icks, Ajay Shah said. Success breeds ar­ro­gance, and the sec­ond sys­tem over­reaches. Multics was the clas­sic case. {032-C04}

brief.head: The man page leads
brief.text: Writing a good man page forces clear think­ing about what a pro­gram should and should not do, Ajay Shah said, and in­vites oth­ers to at­tack it. {032-C11}

brief.head: Name your files well
brief.text: Lowercase for files, up­per­case for di­rec­to­ries, un­der­scores for spa­ces, a README ev­ery­where: Ajay Shah’s de­fence against a for­get­ful mind, with files thirty or forty years old. {032-C18}

brief.head: Impossible, they said
brief.text: Top re­search groups told the Aadhaar team that match­ing any­one against 1.4 bil­lion records could not be done. “They wrote it them­selves and they did it,” Ajay Shah said. {032-S12}

brief.head: Hamming’s prophecy
brief.text: Richard Hamming pre­dicted in the early six­ties that over half of Bell Labs’ work would be com­pu­ta­tion. Every sad grad­u­ate stu­dent now knows it, Ajay Shah said. {032-J04}

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah’s long-promised Unix episode, with Amit Varma
lead.head: Everything is Unix

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 32

body: In an ear­lier episode, Ajay Shah promised to do an episode on Unix if enough view­ers asked for one. They did. Amit Varma in­tro­duced it as one of the great pas­sions of Shah’s life and the driv­ing force of much of his cre­ativ­ity.
Over two hours, the hosts ar­gued that Unix is more than soft­ware. It is the story of a re­mark­able lab, and a phi­los­o­phy that, as Varma put it, one could choose to re­pro­gram one­self through.

And it runs nearly ev­ery­thing. Shah listed Android and iOS phones, the Kindle, the iPad, the servers be­hind Amazon and the cloud. Of the 500 most pow­er­ful com­put­ers in the world, he said, 490 or more run some vari­ant of Unix.
“So there is re­ally no other op­er­at­ing sys­tem other than Unix today,” he said. The one hold­out is Microsoft, whose Windows ma­chines are a de­clin­ing share of the world.
## A spe­cial place

Varma began with Bell Labs, the re­search arm of AT&T where Unix was born. Its se­cret, Shah ar­gued, was not money. Murray Hill had about 3,000 em­ploy­ees, around 1,000 of them PhDs, a scale many or­gan­i­sa­tions, even in India, could af­ford today.
“So it’s not the magic of re­sourc­ing,” he said. “It is some other magic. It’s a magic of cul­ture, it’s a magic of man­age­ment.” {032-C01}

That cul­ture gave Ken Thompson, back from the failed Multics project, the room to build Unix in three weeks on an ob­so­lete com­puter no­body wanted, even though man­age­ment had re­fused to fund op­er­at­ing-systems re­search. {032-S05}
From there, Shah traced the line through the C lan­guage, the uni­ver­si­ties and Berkeley to the in­ter­net, Linux and Apple.
## Why Unix won

Much of the con­ver­sa­tion was about why. Shah’s first an­swer was aes­thetic. Systems built from a few sim­ple com­po­nents, with many fea­tures thrown away, work bet­ter be­cause the human mind can grasp them.
“So I want to use the idea that sim­plic­ity and beauty is the user in­ter­face of the human mind,” he said. {032-C08}
Build one small tool at a time, he said, make it bul­let­proof, and let peo­ple com­bine tools like Lego blocks. Write code as you would write prose. Share it, as sci­en­tists share their proofs.

Varma, who teaches a writ­ing course, said that writ­ing clearly forces you to think clearly, and asked whether pro­gram­ming does the same. “Good pro­gram­mers be­come bet­ter thinkers,” Shah replied. “But it’s got to be done right.”

Shah also ar­gued that Unix and the in­ter­net were built to allow anonymity and en­cryp­tion, and so kept com­put­ing from be­com­ing a strait­jacket con­trolled by cor­po­ra­tions or gov­ern­ments. {032-C16}
## The com­mand line
Then Shah opened a ter­mi­nal. In a screen­cast, he showed how to name files with care, sort a table of the show’s episodes and join com­mands with the pipe.
By the end, view­ers had writ­ten a one-line awk pro­gram. Had they done some­thing clever, or be­come pro­gram­mers? “The an­swer is both,” Shah said.
“This is part of how the Unix world works that pro­gram­ming is for ev­ery­body.” {032-C20}

second.label: Talent spotting
second.head: A forgery that paid off
second.deck: Ajay Shah on the professor who bent the rules for Ken Thompson
body: As an un­der­grad­u­ate at UC Berkeley, Ken Thompson worked on the uni­ver­sity com­puter from mid­night to 8 a.m., when it was all his. When a pro­fes­sor asked whether he would go to grad­u­ate school, Thompson said no. He thought he was just a reg­u­lar guy. {032-S03}
Without telling him, Ajay Shah said, the pro­fes­sor filled in the ap­pli­ca­tion, forged his sig­na­ture and sent it in. Thompson was ac­cepted.

Shah told a sim­i­lar story about his fa­ther, who went back to ed­u­ca­tion through night school and did not get good marks in his master’s at Bombay University. The department’s el­ders, who knew him, took him into the PhD any­way. In India today, Shah said, ev­ery­thing is reg­i­mented. {032-C05}

quote.text: We should al­ways look at the per­son and not at me­chan­i­cal pro­ce­dure.

third.head: Don’t lose heart, Linus

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on his 1991 email to Linus Torvalds

body: In 1991 a young stu­dent in Finland posted on Net News that he had been fool­ing around with the code of Minix and had writ­ten a brand new op­er­at­ing sys­tem. What did peo­ple think? {032-S09}
The reply from Andy Tanenbaum, a great com­puter sci­en­tist, was “ex­tremely mean and crit­i­cal”, Ajay Shah said. Shah, older than Linus Torvalds, thought it un­fair.
“So I wrote email to Linus say­ing you should not be dis­heart­ened. What you’re doing is very im­por­tant,” Shah said.

He booted Linux when it reached ver­sion 0.1. Apart from seven or eight years on Mac OS X, it has been his only sys­tem since. Today, he said, the Linux ker­nel is man­aged by 10,000 or 20,000 pro­gram­mers spread all over the world. {032-C17}

box.title: The memoir behind the episode
box.text: Amit Varma calls Brian Kernighan’s *UNIX: A History and a Memoir* a must-read. For Ajay Shah, it is the source of ori­gin sto­ries from Ken Thompson’s forged ap­pli­ca­tion to his re­cruit­ment by tele­phone. {032-S03}

sections.label: The place
sections.head: A factory for ideas
sections.caption: Bell Labs and its long game
body: Asked where he would go in a time ma­chine, Bill Gates chose Bell Labs in December 1947, Amit Varma said: the month the tran­sis­tor was cre­ated. {#gates}

By the six­ties, AT&T’s re­search lab­o­ra­tory em­ployed more than 15,000 peo­ple. Telephony was a nat­u­ral mo­nop­oly, so AT&T had a guar­an­teed rev­enue stream and could fund work that need not pay off by the next quar­ter.
The num­bers are often over­stated, Varma said. About 2.8 per cent of rev­enues went to R&D, and 0.3 per cent to basic re­search. {#rd} What mat­tered, he said, was the long hori­zon. {032-S01}
## Eccentrics, not dream­ers
It was, Varma said, “a place for ec­centrics but not dream­ers”. You could take the long view, but ideas had to be­come things. {032-C02}

Brian Kernighan, he re­called, was set­tling into his new of­fice when a stranger said: “Hey, I’m Dick, let’s go for lunch.” Only later did he re­alise it was the great Richard Hamming. Kernighan’s ver­dict: ge­og­ra­phy is des­tiny. {032-S02}
Varma’s point was not per­for­ma­tive of­fice at­ten­dance. “The real cre­ativ­ity hap­pens is in the wa­ter­cooler con­ver­sa­tions,” he said. “It’s in the beer after the of­fice work.”
Ajay Shah cred­ited the post-war American mood: bound­less op­ti­mism, a flow­er­ing of free­dom, and lit­tle ac­cep­tance of top-down au­thor­ity on ei­ther side.
~ Shah also praised Varma’s read­ing for the episode: “This boy is not a Bengali dreamer.”

quote.text: This is a broad field we are in. Many things are pos­si­ble. Design the fu­ture.

sections.label: The history
sections.head: C is for Unix
sections.caption: how C and the universities spread Unix
body: After Unix booted, Ajay Shah said, came the story of C. Every op­er­at­ing sys­tem of the age was writ­ten in as­sem­bly lan­guage, which took some­one like Ken Thompson.
Dennis Ritchie asked whether Unix could be writ­ten in a high-level lan­guage. None was good enough, so he and oth­ers built a new one. {032-S07}
“And C was writ­ten to make it pos­si­ble to write Unix in C,” Shah said. Rewritten, Unix could move to more and more ma­chines.
## Antitrust to the res­cue

AT&T could have launched its own com­put­ers and be­come a mo­nop­oly in com­put­ing too. Shah’s opin­ion is that its bat­tles with an­titrust au­thor­i­ties stopped it. {032-S08} It sent Unix to uni­ver­si­ties in­stead, under a li­cence to read and tin­ker but not com­mer­cialise.
A fa­mous book printed the ker­nel with a line-by-line com­men­tary. At Berkeley, Bill Joy con­nected Unix to net­work­ing, and it car­ried TCP/IP and the in­ter­net.

Steve Jobs chose BSD Unix at NeXT and brought the NeXT team back to Apple. He had re­lied on ad­vis­ers he trusted, Shah said, until iTunes was writ­ten in roughly a week: “Steve Jobs is said to have got re­li­gion.” {032-S10}
~ There are grum­blers, Shah said, who say Unix is hold­ing us back, and he has no doubt that the next gen­er­a­tion must be found.

quote.text: I want to claim some credit for the econ­o­mists here.

sections.label: The philosophy
sections.head: Beauty is a working part
sections.caption: simplicity, small tools and prose
body: Why did Unix win? Ajay Shah began with an aes­thetic sense of sim­plic­ity. He quoted the com­puter sci­en­tist David Gelernter: “When faced with com­plex­ity, our only de­fence is beauty.” {032-J14}

His sec­ond prin­ci­ple was to build one small tool at a time, lim­ited but bul­let­proof, and let peo­ple com­bine tools like Lego blocks, rather than run one giant top-down project. His own method is to think long with a prob­lem “up­loaded” in his brain, then solve the hard­est pieces first. {032-C09}
## Prose and code

Third came writ­ing. Bell Labs wrote terse, pre­cise man pages and slim books, and its peo­ple im­proved each other’s drafts. “Writing code is like writ­ing prose,” Shah said. “They’re not dif­fer­ent.” {032-C10}
Amit Varma added Deirdre McCloskey, for whom writ­ing is part of re­search, and Joan Didion: “I don’t know what I think till I write it down.” {032-J15}

Shah ques­tioned any­one who shelves cul­ture and phi­los­o­phy apart from en­gi­neer­ing. In India’s doc­tor-engineer world, he said, the sep­a­ra­tion has cost en­gi­neers their sense of good en­gi­neer­ing.

~ Following Donald Knuth, he said, code should ex­plain the al­go­rithm to a per­son sit­ting be­side you. Badly writ­ten code is thrown away within a year; the Unix com­mu­nity is tend­ing “a gar­den with fifty-year-old trees”.

quote.text: It’s good to find the hard­est things and solve them and get them done.

portraits.caption: Joan Didion
portraits.credit: Kathleen Ballard, Los Angeles Times, CC BY 4.0

sections.label: The commons
sections.head: Science by another name
sections.caption: open source and public goods
body: At Bell Labs, Ajay Shah said, shar­ing code came nat­u­rally. It was the cul­ture of sci­ence and math­e­mat­ics: if I prove a the­o­rem, I show you the proof. {032-C13}
The open source move­ment, he said, is just the con­tin­u­a­tion of a story that began five hun­dred years ago, when Newton pub­lished his proofs and demon­stra­tions.

In the mid-1970s, by Shah’s ac­count, Bill Gates wrote a man­i­festo for se­cret com­mer­cial soft­ware and Richard Stallman a rival one for soft­ware as open as math­e­mat­ics and physics. At one point, he thought, Microsoft made 90 per cent of all the com­puter companies’ prof­its. {#microsoft} Yet it never de­vel­oped a new idea.
## A real pub­lic good

Downloaded code is non-rival and non-excludable, Shah ar­gued: a pub­lic good. The US Department of Defense funded TCP/IP and AT&T paid the early salaries, but no gov­ern­ment con­trols Unix or the in­ter­net. {032-C14}

Amit Varma saw mar­kets in the broad sense: vol­un­tary co­op­er­a­tion. One of Shah’s clos­ing picks, Eric Raymond’s essay *The Cathedral & the Bazaar*, asks how un­paid vol­un­teers build such soft­ware: “It’s like you’re not pay­ing, but they’re build­ing the world’s best soft­ware.” {032-R09}
~ And for the Indian na­tion­al­ists, Shah added: “Nobody called it America Stack, they just called it Unix and the Internet.” {032-J06}

quote.text: I think Unix and the in­ter­net are dig­i­tal pub­lic goods. There’s no gov­ern­ment in the pic­ture.

sections.label: The freedom
sections.head: Four rupees an email
sections.caption: freedom wired into the internet
body: An op­er­at­ing sys­tem can eas­ily exert dra­co­nian con­trol, Ajay Shah said, and com­put­ing could have be­come a strait­jacket. Unix and the in­ter­net in­stead ac­cepted a great deal of an­ar­chism: anony­mous use, en­cryp­tion, VPNs. {032-C16}

Picture the al­ter­na­tive, he said: a WhatsApp uncle de­mand­ing a UID iris scan every time you switch on your phone, “be­cause oth­er­wise ter­ror­ists will use phones”, and four ru­pees charged for each email. {032-J05}
Spam is the price of open email, Shah con­ceded. It is still bet­ter, he said, than claus­tro­pho­bic con­trol.
## Stubborn fru­gal­ity

Decades of clever peo­ple on un­der­pow­ered ma­chines have sharp­ened Unix’s al­go­rithms, he said, so it does more with less hard­ware, and old com­put­ers headed for the bin can be re­vived. {032-C15}

Amit Varma asked what a nor­mal per­son could do. Shah asked for prac­ti­cal­ity: “show me where is the beef, or show me where is the ras­gulla?” Varma ruled that anti-national and un­healthy. {032-J02}
~ Shah’s an­swer: watch, and join, the Linux kernel’s open de­vel­op­ment through Git, and play with a Raspberry Pi, a credit card-sized com­puter cost­ing a few thou­sand ru­pees. {#raspberry}

quote.text: The in­ter­net is deeply wired for free, flex­i­ble, anony­mous use.

sections.label: The screencast
sections.head: Pipe dreams
sections.caption: the Unix command line
body: In his screen­cast, Ajay Shah set graph­i­cal ap­pli­ca­tions like LibreOffice and Chrome aside. They run on any Unix ma­chine, he said, but the in­ter­est­ing work hap­pens at the com­mand line.

He walked through his di­rec­tory for the show, with a README to guide his fu­ture self, then sorted a table of 23 episodes by length. The short­est ran 46 min­utes; Ukraine, at 91, was the long­est. {#ukraine}
The pipe joins com­mands: the out­put of sort goes to tail, which keeps the last three lines. Data stays in plain text, never in a for­mat only one pro­gram can read. {032-C19}
## One line, one in­sight

With awk, Shah worked out min­utes per viewer. In June 2023, about 300 hours went to 1,947 unique view­ers, nine min­utes each, mostly cu­ri­ous spec­ta­tors. By November, some 14,000 view­ers av­er­aged about 45 min­utes. {032-S13}
The early in­for­ma­tion prob­lem had re­ceded, he thought: peo­ple now knew what the show was, and kept com­ing back.
~ He also wrapped Pandoc, a con­verter from every file for­mat to every other, into a new com­mand of his own, so that Amit Varma, who does not use Emacs, could get Word files.

quote.text: Plain text files are the uni­ver­sal lan­guage by which all the pro­grams speak to each other
So we can just go look at the sausage fac­tory, we can see what is being done by who and how, and then we can start par­tic­i­pat­ing and we can start con­tribut­ing.

p3.title: Tales from the lab
p3.deck: A junked computer, a motel, a patent office and a chess game

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how a space game became an operating system
stories.head: Junk in, Unix out
body: Bell Labs had been burned by Multics. Its man­agers, Ajay Shah said, would hire all kinds of crazy peo­ple, but they were not going to fund op­er­at­ing sys­tems. You could fool around on your own time; se­ri­ous re­sourc­ing was out.

Ken Thompson, back from the failed project, found an ob­so­lete PDP-7 lying in a cor­ner. It had per­haps 16 or 32 kilo­bytes of mem­ory, Shah said, and a disk that was too fast for the com­puter. {#memory}
Thompson wrote a space travel game on it, in which you flew a space­craft and tried to land on Jupiter. Brian Kernighan, Shah said, writes that he played it and en­joyed it.
Fighting with that disk, Thompson wrote a disk-scheduling al­go­rithm, a file sys­tem and a de­vice driver. Then he un­der­stood that he was three weeks from an op­er­at­ing sys­tem.

His wife and child hap­pened to be going to California to visit his par­ents. “He planned it as one week to write an ed­i­tor, one week to write an as­sem­bler, one week to write the op­er­at­ing sys­tem ker­nel, in three weeks I’ll be done,” Shah said. {032-S05}
It worked out ex­actly like that. Unix booted. It was bare and stripped down, and its name was a nod to the failed Multics.
~ Every of­fice, Shah ob­served, has a sup­ply of rub­bish no­body is using, and this story “runs con­trary to any de­clut­ter man­i­festo”: you do want to keep your PDP-7s. {032-J03}
stories.why: Junk hard­ware, no fund­ing and three weeks alone pro­duced Unix. Amit Varma called it danc­ing with chains: a too-fast disk and a bor­rowed bud­get pushed cre­ativ­ity along rather than stop­ping it. {#chains}
stories.postscript: Thompson, Shah re­called, said the next rev­o­lu­tion will start with a space travel game on some de­funct Cray-1 su­per­com­puter.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Ken Thompson’s three weeks

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the recruitment of Ken Thompson
stories.head: Every motel in New Jersey
body: Ken Thompson told Bell Labs he would never work for a cor­po­ra­tion. He was a re­searcher and a thinker, Ajay Shah said, and com­pa­nies were no good.
Bell Labs kept after him and flew him east to give a talk. In the cor­ri­dor, read­ing the names on the doors, he thought how amaz­ing it would be to be near these peo­ple. {#corridor}
After the talk he drove to a friend’s house, where a printed offer reached him, then on to a motel, still un­de­cided. Bell Labs called him there too. How, he asked, had they found him?
“Well, we’re the tele­phone com­pany,” came the an­swer. “We found the phone num­ber of every motel in New Jersey and we made all the calls and we found you.” {032-S04} He ac­cepted.
~ And that, Shah said, is how Thompson joined Bell Labs.
stories.why: Talent pulls in tal­ent. It was the names on the doors, the clus­ter­ing and net­work ef­fects, Ajay Shah said, that drew Thompson in; the tele­phone company’s per­sis­tence did the rest.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the call to every motel

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on funding an operating system by stealth
stories.head: Smuggled in as patent software
body: Even after Unix booted, Bell Labs man­age­ment re­fused to fund op­er­at­ing sys­tems, Ajay Shah said, be­cause of the money wasted on Multics.

Then the group had a brain­wave. Bell Labs was run­ning at about one patent a day, and patent ap­pli­ca­tions needed strict for­mat­ting, di­a­grams and equa­tions. Management was about to pay an out­side ven­dor for a sys­tem that type­set patents. {#patent}

The Unix group of­fered to build one in-house for the same money. What they knew in their minds was that they would write a whole doc­u­ment-processing sys­tem, run it on Unix and build Unix out on mod­ern hard­ware. Management ap­proved. {032-S06}
~ The tools were roff, then nroff, then troff, which em­bed­ded com­mands for ital­ics, bold­face and sec­tion num­bers in raw text. The word “markup” in HTML, Shah said, orig­i­nates here.
stories.why: When man­agers will not back the bet you be­lieve in, find a prob­lem they will pay for, one where your bet is the cheap­est so­lu­tion. Unix was built out on a type­set­ting bud­get.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the patent-typesetting gambit

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on why play is a good use of a mind
stories.head: Cute, but is it useful?
body: A pow­er­ful vis­i­tor was tour­ing Bell Labs with its pres­i­dent, Ajay Shah re­called, when Ken Thompson showed him a pro­gram that played chess. “Yeah, this is cute,” the vis­i­tor said, “but how is it use­ful?” {#chess}

Thompson had brought dy­namic pro­gram­ming to the chess endgame, list­ing every mat­ing po­si­tion and work­ing back­wards. The idea came from Richard Bellman and Robert Kalaba at the RAND Corporation. Kalaba, Shah said, was his teacher, and his own PhD the­sis, on women in Malaysia, rested on dy­namic pro­gram­ming.

The pres­i­dent of Bell Labs had an an­swer: al­go­rithms de­vel­oped along the way helped sched­ule phone calls in the Bell sys­tem. Management, Shah said, would not fund an op­er­at­ing sys­tem, but it never stopped any­one writ­ing one. {032-S11}
~ Amit Varma added that endgames with seven pieces or fewer are now ba­si­cally solved, using table­bases.

quote.text: build­ing a space travel game and a chess pro­gram is ac­tu­ally a good use of the human mind

quiz.q: Why, according to Ajay Shah, did Bell Labs succeed, given that its budget was not exceptional?
quiz.a: Its cul­ture and man­age­ment, not its re­sources: many or­gan­i­sa­tions could fund one today.

quiz.q: Ken Thompson was undecided, staying at a motel. How did Bell Labs track him down?
quiz.a: As the tele­phone com­pany, it phoned every motel in New Jersey until it found him.

quiz.q: How did Ken Thompson divide the three weeks his family spent visiting his parents in California?
quiz.a: One week each for an ed­i­tor, an as­sem­bler and the op­er­at­ing sys­tem ker­nel.

quiz.q: Which programming language did Dennis Ritchie and others create, and why?
quiz.a: C, to make it pos­si­ble to write Unix in a high-level lan­guage.

quiz.q: What made Steve Jobs, by Ajay Shah’s account, finally get religion about Unix?
quiz.a: iTunes was writ­ten in roughly a week on Apple’s new Unix en­vi­ron­ment.

quiz.q: What did Ajay Shah’s one-line awk program reveal about viewers of the show?
quiz.a: Minutes per unique viewer rose from nine in June to about 45 by November.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 32. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Steve Jobs (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0); Brian Kernighan (Thiele41, CC BY-SA 3.0); Ken Thompson (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Dennis M. Ritchie (Denise Panyik-Dale, CC BY 2.0); Bill Joy (The original uploader was SqueakBox at English Wikipedia., CC BY 2.0); Donald Knuth (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.5); Joan Didion (Kathleen Ballard, Los Angeles Times, CC BY 4.0); Richard Stallman (Patafisik, CC BY-SA 4.0); Neal Stephenson (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0).

shelf.title: The Idea Factory: Bell Labs and the Great Age of American Innovation
shelf.creator: Jon Gertner
shelf.why: It ex­plains how a lab that played the long game pro­duced ideas that be­came the foun­da­tion of the mod­ern world.

shelf.title: UNIX: A History and a Memoir
shelf.creator: Brian Kernighan
shelf.why: He calls it a must-read his­tory of Unix by an in­sider who ex­plains why the Bell Labs cul­ture worked.

shelf.title: UNIX: A History and a Memoir
shelf.creator: Brian Kernighan
shelf.why: A brief his­tory of the early years of Unix and Bell Labs, and the source of sev­eral ori­gin sto­ries Ajay tells, in­clud­ing Thompson’s forged ap­pli­ca­tion and his re­cruit­ment.

shelf.title: The Design of Everyday Things
shelf.creator: Don Norman
shelf.why: Norman shows that ev­ery­thing around us looks and works the way it does for rea­sons we have stopped notic­ing, and that noth­ing is beau­ti­ful un­less it is also beau­ti­fully func­tional, a les­son for en­gi­neer­ing too.

shelf.title: The Elements of Programming Style
shelf.creator: Brian Kernighan and PJ Plauger
shelf.why: It car­ries the val­ues of good prose into code: sim­plic­ity, el­e­gance, being easy to un­der­stand, and not a word out of place.

shelf.title: The Elements of Style
shelf.creator: William Strunk and EB White
shelf.why: The clas­sic state­ment of clar­ity and brevity, val­ues Bell Labs car­ried into pro­gram­ming; Ajay says ‘the sim­ple Strunk and White’ should be uni­ver­sal knowl­edge for ev­ery­one doing re­search.

shelf.title: Numerical Methods for Scientists and Engineers
shelf.creator: Richard Hamming
shelf.why: It is by one of Bell Labs’ great fig­ures, the man Amit quotes as say­ing that the pur­pose of com­put­ing is in­sight, not num­bers.

shelf.title: In the Beginning...Was the Command Line
shelf.creator: Neal Stephenson
shelf.why: It is not an en­gi­neer­ing book.

shelf.title: The Cathedral & the Bazaar
shelf.creator: Eric S Raymond
shelf.why: Raymond’s ac­count of why Unix and open source work: the teem­ing, ar­gu­ing bazaar of un­paid vol­un­teers beats a few great peo­ple build­ing a cathe­dral.

shelf.title: A Commentary on the UNIX Operating System
shelf.creator: John Lions
shelf.why: It is how uni­ver­si­ties world­wide learned how an op­er­at­ing sys­tem is ac­tu­ally writ­ten, which made Unix their com­mon lan­guage.

shelf.title: Raspberry Pi 4
shelf.why: Ajay calls it the best bang for the buck and says it’s a de­light.

shelf.title: A router that runs an open-source version of Unix
shelf.why: You can tin­ker with the soft­ware that runs your own net­work hard­ware.

shelf.title: Pandoc
shelf.why: He calls it a Swiss Army knife that con­verts any file for­mat to any other from the com­mand line, and it can be wrapped into your own au­to­mated com­mands.

shelf.title: Emacs (org mode)
shelf.why: Ajay’s ed­i­tor of choice: a fifty-year-old, fully pro­gram­mable tool whose age has pro­duced el­e­gant de­sign and bul­let­proof code.

shelf.title: awk
shelf.why: Its pat­tern-and-action model lets you do se­ri­ous data pro­cess­ing in one line.

shelf.title: make
shelf.why: Another good tool for au­tomat­ing your own work.

shelf.title: Top500.org
shelf.why: Of the 500 most pow­er­ful com­put­ers in the world, roughly 490 or more run some vari­ant of Unix.

shelf.title: Shane Parrish’s tweet on working from home
shelf.creator: Shane Parrish
shelf.why: Its gist is that peo­ple who show up at the of­fice will end up as bosses of those who work from home.

shelf.title: Why Talent Comes in Clusters (Episode 8)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why the bright­est peo­ple con­cen­trate in places like Silicon Valley and Bell Labs, and how a clus­ter be­comes a mag­net for more tal­ent, helped by friendly reg­u­la­tion and a cul­ture where it is okay to fail.

shelf.title: Seven Stories That Should Be Films (Episode 23)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The first of the show’s se­ries of true sto­ries the hosts would turn into films, and Amit’s favourite episode at the time.

shelf.title: Math Is Better Than the Brigadier’s Girlfriend (Episode 15)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: An early episode that the hosts cite as in-person col­lab­o­ra­tion at its best, and as back­ground for the Data General con­nec­tion Ajay draws later.

shelf.title: Declutter (Episode 30)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Much of the hosts’ per­sonal phi­los­o­phy of life: recog­nise your con­straints, es­pe­cially time, pri­ori­tise ac­cord­ingly, and pre­fer pro­cesses to grand goals.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: The Art of Clear Writing
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s writ­ing course, which treats clear writ­ing as a test of clear think­ing.

laughs.text: After list­ing Amit’s re­search, Ajay says: ‘This boy is not a Bengali dreamer. Look at the num­ber of books he has read for this one episode. Get off your butt and read some books.’ Amit replies: ‘I am Bengali in the sense that I would urge my gen­tle read­ers, don’t get off your butt. It’s a very com­fort­able place. God gave you a butt for a rea­son, right? Actually God gave you a butt for two rea­sons.’

Ajay de­mands prac­ti­cal­ity: ‘show me where is the beef, or show me where is the ras­gulla?’ Amit re­sponds: ‘What you said was firstly anti-national and sec­ondly un­healthy. No ras­gul­las, too much sugar.’

On the PDP-7 found in a cor­ner, Ajay says every of­fice has a sup­ply of un­used rub­bish, and ‘this story runs con­trary to any de­clut­ter man­i­festo that you do want to keep your PDP 7s’, a jab at their own Declutter episode.

Ajay on Hamming’s pre­dic­tion that com­pu­ta­tion would take over sci­ence: every sad grad­u­ate stu­dent learns it. ‘You may think you’re doing bi­ol­ogy, you may think you’re doing po­lit­i­cal sci­ence. Ghoom phir ke, it’s just pro­gram­ming.’

Ajay’s WhatsApp-uncle dystopia: an uncle in­sist­ing on an Aadhaar iris scan every time you switch on your phone ‘be­cause oth­er­wise ter­ror­ists will use phones’. He adds a world where you must scan your iris be­fore email­ing and are ‘charged four ru­pees for each email’.
A jab at India Stack na­tion­al­ism: ‘for all the Indian na­tion­al­ists, Nobody called it America Stack, they just called it Unix and the Internet.’
Bill Gates, asked where he would go in a time ma­chine, chose Bell Labs in December 1947, when the tran­sis­tor was cre­ated.

Arthur C. Clarke on Bell Labs’ New Jersey site: it looks like a large, mod­ern fac­tory, but it is a fac­tory for ideas whose pro­duc­tion lines are in­vis­i­ble. Jon Gertner took his book’s title from this.
Amit’s favourite de­scrip­tion of why Multics failed: it was try­ing to climb many trees at the same time.

The word ‘markup’ in HTML (hy­per­text markup lan­guage) traces back to Bell Labs’ roff/nroff/troff type­set­ting tools, which em­bed­ded com­mands for ital­ics, bold­face and sec­tion num­bers in raw text.
Richard Hamming: ‘The pur­pose of com­put­ing is in­sight, not num­bers.’ He also pre­dicted in the early six­ties that more than half of Bell Labs’ work would turn out to be com­pu­ta­tion.
David Gelernter: ‘When faced with com­plex­ity, our only de­fense is beauty.’
Bill Gates and Richard Stallman’s rival man­i­festos of the mid-1970s, se­cret com­mer­cial soft­ware ver­sus soft­ware as open as math­e­mat­ics and physics, a split Ajay says has run ever since.

Ken Thompson’s prophecy, as Ajay re­counts it: some­where a de­funct Cray-1 su­per­com­puter sits un­used in a lab, and the next Ken Thompson will write a space travel game on it and start the next rev­o­lu­tion in com­put­ing.
